name: Executive order of February 12, 1875 establishing the Lemhi Valley Indian Reservation
nations: Lemhi Shoshone (Lemhi Tribe), with Sheepeater (Tukuarika, as the Commission spells it) and Bannock people, represented today by the Shoshone-Bannock Tribes of the Fort Hall Reservation
promises: The President established the Lemhi Valley Indian Reservation in Idaho for the mixed tribes of Shoshone, Bannock and Sheepeater Indians (Docket 326 findings, 1962).

Royce records that the reserve took the place of the one described in an earlier unratified treaty, under which the Indians had agreed to cede all land outside a two-township reserve on the North Fork of the Salmon River above Fort Lemhi.

breaches.what: The Commission found that the Lemhi Tribe held aboriginal title to its lands and that the United States acquired those lands without paying compensation on February 12, 1875, the date this order set up the Lemhi reserve.

landTaken: The Lemhi aboriginal lands described in the Commission's 1962 findings (acreage not recorded here). By an agreement of May 14, 1880, ratified by the Act of February 23, 1889, 25 Stat. 687, the Lemhi agreed to give up the reserve and move to Fort Hall, and they moved in 1907 (Docket 326 findings, 1962).
compensation: Compromise settlement in Docket 326-I (1971) for a net final judgment of $4,500,000.00, the figure written in the tribal resolution and the Interior Department letter set out in the Commission's findings on the compromise. The stipulation says it is not an admission by either party.
today: The Lemhi reserve no longer exists; its people moved to the Fort Hall Reservation in 1907 (Docket 326 findings, 1962).

openQuestions: No Shoshone-Bannock Tribes page about the Lemhi removal of 1907 was found on the tribes' site.
The order's own text (Kappler vol. 1, p. 839) was not opened; it is described here from the Commission's findings and Royce.

Audit 2026-11-08: the settlement figure was added: the findings on the compromise (ICC pointer 1514) print "$4,500,000.00" cleanly in the tribal resolution and the Interior Department letter; only the final award's scan of the figure is damaged.
Audit 2026-11-08: Royce dates the unratified treaty this reserve replaced to September 24, 1868 (Royce schedule, remark opposite the order of February 12, 1875).

nationVoice.summary: At the Tribes' 2021 Virginia City Treaty Day gathering, reported by the Sho-Ban News, tribal attorney Jeanette Wolfley said the 1875 executive order establishing the Lemhi Reservation did not end Agai Deka use of their southwest Montana lands, that some Agai Deka were forcibly removed to Fort Hall in 1905 while Chief Tendoy refused to relocate, and that the Tribes hold their aboriginal title there was never given up; Chairman Devon Boyer said the government took what it wanted no matter what the people said.

plain.promised: Not a treaty: an executive order. The President established the Lemhi Valley Indian Reservation in Idaho for the mixed tribes of Shoshone, Bannock and Sheepeater Indians.
plain.happened: The Indian Claims Commission found in 1962 that the United States acquired the Lemhi Tribe's aboriginal lands without paying compensation on February 12, 1875, the date of this order.
plain.today: The claim was settled by compromise in 1971 for a net $4,500,000.00, not an admission by either party. Whether it was paid has not been traced. The Lemhi people moved to the Fort Hall Reservation in 1907.
